_doc: Carriage modes. crew_trade: the trade whose hours drive the carrier (the labour package counts them as carriage need). edge_classes: land, river, coast, open_sea. requires_nodes: tech nodes a party must hold to use the mode. needs_improvement: key the caller's improvements dict must carry on the edge (built roads and track). model picks the physics in sim/geography/routes_rates.py and carrier holds its inputs. critical_grade: grade at which pace halves. max_grade: grade above which the mode cannot be used. built_grade_cap: grade a built improvement is levelled to; max_natural_grade: steepest natural grade it can be built over without an 'engineered' improvement. km_factor: share of the edge's km a built way keeps. engineered: {max_grade, earthwork_factor, kind, conf, source, why} lets a built way cross ground steeper than max_natural_grade up to max_grade, with the cut-and-fill bench multiplied by earthwork_factor (cuttings, embankments, retaining walls); the caller records the edge as engineered. river_crossing: how a land mode meets a river crossing (a land edge between tiles on the same river): absent means the carrier fords or ferries it, paying the mode's own handling once; "bridge_only" means it cannot cross without a built bridge; "none" means the mode's works carry their own crossings. carries: the cargo classes the mode takes (absent means every class): "goods" for carried freight, "living_stock" for animals, which can be shipped on water and rail but on land walk themselves (the droving mode). cargo_walks: the cargo is the carrier (a herd driven to market), so its feed is eaten on the loaded leg only and no carrier capital is charged. cargo_loss_per_day (with cargo_loss_conf and cargo_loss_source): the share of the cargo lost each day on the road, counted in the cargo's cost share. handling_hours_per_tonne and handling_days: load and unload each time a haul changes to this mode. dues_hours_per_tonne (with dues_conf and dues_source): tolls or port dues charged on the same occasion; absent means none.

entries.label: Porters on foot
entries.source: Research notes section 3: porters carry 25 to 30 kg at 20 to 25 km a day. Tlameme (Mexica porters) carried on average 23 kg and covered 21 to 25 km a day: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tlamemeh ("carrying on average 23 kilos", "daily commute of 21 to 25 kilometers"; a secondary source, Hassig not opened). Cross-checks opened, none replacing the figures: Law and Rodway, Himalayan Journal 64 (2008), "Lowland porters in the Solu Khumbu" (Nepal, commercial porters, "a 24 year old man who weighed 52 kg carrying a 90 kg load from Jiri to Kakou, a six-day walk"; industry limit for trekking porters "30 kg per porter"; no km a day given); an Infobae article (2022) gives "about 23 kg" and "between 21 and 28 km" for the Mexica with no source of its own.
entries.why: Carriage with no animal and no road, available on any land edge.

closures.source: Alpine and Pyrenean passes (Great St Bernard, Septimer, Somport) were shut or barely passable by snow from about November to April; porters kept crossing in snow with delay. Thresholds on tile mean elevation and coldest-month temperature stand in for a pass-level snow layer.
closures.why: A cargo on a high cold edge waits for the thaw or goes round; an edge is taken to be a pass when the higher end tile is mountainous and the colder end is below freezing in winter.

entries.label: Pack animals
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: road, bridge and gate tolls, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py pack_freight_physical_inputs; grade limits from research notes section 2.
entries.why: Caravans and mule strings cross rough country without a road.

closures.source: Alpine and Pyrenean passes (Great St Bernard, Septimer, Somport) were shut or barely passable by snow from about November to April; mule strings kept crossing in snow with delay. Thresholds on tile mean elevation and coldest-month temperature stand in for a pass-level snow layer.
closures.why: A cargo on a high cold edge waits for the thaw or goes round; an edge is taken to be a pass when the higher end tile is mountainous and the colder end is below freezing in winter.

entries.label: Droving live animals
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: road, bridge and gate tolls, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode.
entries.cargo_loss_source: Labelled heuristic: the herd loses a thousandth of its number and weight a day to straying, injury and wasting on the road; drovers held the pace down because a herd driven harder lost weight and was hard to sell. Not fitted to a record.
entries.source: Pace and herd size: drovers kept cattle to 10 to 15 miles a day or they lost weight (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Droving, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_drives_in_the_United_States); a Kentucky-style drive was 100 to 120 head with three drovers, so about 35 head a drover (popular summaries, not primary records). The herd's feed comes from sim/geography/droving.py: maintenance and the work of walking, in the draught ox's feed terms; the animal is a stand-in for the herd.
entries.why: Live animals walk to market at the cost of their own feed and the drovers' days, with the daily loss counted against the cargo, not carried at freight rates.

closures.source: Alpine and Pyrenean passes (Great St Bernard, Septimer, Somport) were shut or barely passable by snow from about November to April; herds were driven over the passes only between the thaw and the first snow. Thresholds on tile mean elevation and coldest-month temperature stand in for a pass-level snow layer.
closures.why: A cargo on a high cold edge waits for the thaw or goes round; an edge is taken to be a pass when the higher end tile is mountainous and the colder end is below freezing in winter.

entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py draught_freight_physical_inputs; wheeled critical slopes from research notes section 2.
entries.why: Wheeled carriage on the unbuilt track between tiles; mountains stop it.

closures.source: Alpine and Pyrenean passes (Great St Bernard, Septimer, Somport) were shut or barely passable by snow from about November to April; wheeled carts stopped altogether and goods were transshipped to pack animals or sledges. Thresholds on tile mean elevation and coldest-month temperature stand in for a pass-level snow layer.

entries.label: Carts on a built road

engineered.source: Labelled heuristic: a cutting or embankment through ground steeper than the natural limit moves a multiple of the side-hill bench, with retaining walls and rock work. Not fitted to a source.
engineered.why: Lets a road be carried over steep ground at a higher earthwork cost.

construction.source: Labelled heuristic: the crew is the labourers one project can work at once and the working days a year are a round figure, so the build time is the person-days over the crew's days in a year; a metalled road a cart can use is a few metres of carriageway on a levelled bed with a stone surface; hand excavation of a few cubic metres a person-day is the order of ancient earthwork rates. Not fitted to a source.
construction.why: What building a road costs per km from its width, bed and surface; the relief adds a cut-and-fill bench (see sim/geography/ways_build.py).

entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: road, bridge and gate tolls, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py PAVED_ROAD; Roman road grades of 4 to 12 percent and circuity 1.1 to 1.2 from research notes sections 2 and 5.
entries.why: A built road lowers rolling resistance, is levelled to a gentler grade and runs straighter than a track.

closures.source: Alpine and Pyrenean passes (Great St Bernard, Septimer, Somport) were shut or barely passable by snow from about November to April; a maintained road was kept open longer than a track. Thresholds on tile mean elevation and coldest-month temperature stand in for a pass-level snow layer.
closures.why: A cargo on a high cold edge waits for the thaw or goes round; an edge is taken to be a pass when the higher end tile is mountainous and the colder end is below freezing in winter.

entries.label: Steam railway

engineered.source: Labelled heuristic: a cutting or embankment through ground steeper than the natural limit moves a multiple of the side-hill bench, with retaining walls and rock work. Not fitted to a source.
engineered.why: Lets a railway be carried over steep ground at a higher earthwork cost.

construction.source: Labelled heuristic: the crew is the labourers one project can work at once and the working days a year are a round figure, so the build time is the person-days over the crew's days in a year; two iron edge rails of a few tens of kilograms a metre on a ballasted bed. Not fitted to a source.
construction.why: What laying a railway costs per km from its bed, ballast and rails; the relief adds a cut-and-fill bench (see sim/geography/ways_build.py).

entries.source: Research notes sections 3 and 5: early steam trains at 30 to 40 km/h, ruling grades of 1 to 1.5 percent, steel-on-steel rolling resistance 0.1 to 0.2 percent; engine efficiency of a few percent. The rolling stock (a mass of locomotive and wagons per tonne of cargo, in iron, and a service life in kilometres) is a labelled heuristic that prices the train as a freight carrier (sim/geography/rail_freight.py).
entries.why: Needs built track; the ruling grade bounds the line, so steeper natural ground needs earthwork.

entries.label: River boats
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: river tolls at bridges, weirs and lock or staithe stations, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.why: Towed barges; the current speeds the way down and slows the way up.

closures.source: Rhine, Danube, Seine and Volga navigation stopped for ice for weeks to months in hard winters; the Hanseatic and Russian river trades paused for the freeze.
closures.why: A river edge with a hard winter waits for the ice to clear; coldest-month temperature stands in for an ice layer.

entries.label: Barges on a canal

engineered.source: Labelled heuristic: a canal over steeper ground is stepped by flights of locks and cut through the rise. Not fitted to a source.
engineered.why: Lets a canal climb ground steeper than the natural limit at a higher earthwork cost.

construction.source: Labelled heuristic: a towpath barge canal of a few metres' depth and a dozen metres' width, cut by hand, with stone revetment and lock gates of timber; the crew and working days are round figures as for a road. Not fitted to a source.
construction.why: What cutting a canal costs per km from its channel and lining; the relief adds a cut-and-fill bench (see sim/geography/ways_build.py).

entries.source: sim/geography/transport.py barge_freight_physical_inputs, towed along the bank on still water.
entries.why: Towed barges on a built channel: still water at the levelled grade, so no current helps or hinders.

entries.label: Sailing ships
entries.dues_source: Labelled heuristic, no per-tonne tariff in hand: harbour, anchorage and quay dues, as unskilled hours per tonne each time a haul changes to the mode. State customs on goods crossing a border (the Roman portoria at a fortieth) are the civilisation's own import and export duty in its state_revenue data, not charged here.
entries.source: sim/geography/sea_freight.py; coast-hugging is slower than open-water sailing per research notes section 6.
entries.why: Wind-driven hulls between ports; both ends of a leg are coastal tiles.

closures.source: Vegetius, Epitoma rei militaris 4.39: the sea is shut from 11 November to 10 March (about 120 days), doubtful in the weeks either side; Pliny, Natural History 2.47 gives the same winter closure.
closures.why: Open-water crossings of the Mediterranean wait for the sailing season.

closures.source: Coasting kept going in winter in fair spells but with far fewer sailings than open-water crossings; half the open-water closure of Vegetius, Epitoma rei militaris 4.39, is a labelled guess.
closures.why: Coast legs of the Mediterranean are slowed by winter weather but not shut.

closures.source: Baltic and White Sea harbours froze for three to five months; Hanseatic sailing paused from about November to March.
closures.why: Sea edges whose coastal tiles have a hard winter wait for the ice to clear; the coldest-month temperature stands in for a sea-ice layer.

closures.source: Periplus Maris Erythraei 57 and Casson's notes: ships leave Egypt for India with the south-west monsoon in July and return with the north-east in winter; a given direction is open about half the year.
closures.why: A crossing of the Indian Ocean waits for the wind that blows its way; averaged over directions the passage is shut about half the year.

entries.source: Research notes section 3: early steamships carry 1 to 3 kt at 250 to 400 km a day, coal heavy on long voyages.
entries.why: Engine-driven hulls ignore the wind and can stem a river current.
